core: Nouns as naming words (people, places, things, ideas)
Common vs proper nouns and capitalization
Plural formation: regular -s/-es and common irregulars
Possessive forms: singular and plural apostrophes
Noun sentence jobs: subject, object, object of a preposition
supporting: Quantity expressions for noncount nouns (a piece of, a bit of)
Dictionary use to check plural and possessive spellings
outOfScope: Pronouns and pronoun-antecedent agreement — separate topic

claims.claim: A noun is a word that names people, places, things, or ideas; nouns can name visible things such as a student or a paper clip, or ideas such as knowledge or democracy.
Proper nouns name specific people, places, things, or ideas and are capitalized; common nouns name general people, places, things, or ideas and are not capitalized unless they begin a sentence.
Concrete nouns name physical entities that can in principle be observed with the senses, while abstract nouns name ideas or concepts; some nouns, such as art, have both concrete and abstract uses.

Count nouns can be expressed in plural form, usually with -s (cat/cats, student/students); noncount nouns name things seen as a whole or mass and usually have no plural form (milk, water, air, money, food).
Most nouns form the plural by adding -s; nouns ending in -s, -ss, -ch, -sh, or -x add -es instead (bus/buses, church/churches, box/boxes).
Some common nouns form irregular plurals that must be memorized, such as foot/feet, mouse/mice, person/people, and child/children.
A few nouns keep the same form in singular and plural (zero inflection), such as sheep, deer, and fish.

Possession is shown with an apostrophe: a singular owner takes 's (Adrian's car); a plural owner that ends in -s takes only the apostrophe (three companies' profits); a plural owner that does not end in -s takes 's (children's fevers).

Nouns perform sentence jobs: the subject is the noun or pronoun the sentence is about; an object is on the receiving end of the verb; the noun that follows a preposition is the object of that preposition and is never the subject.
Quantity words connect to countability: much modifies only noncount nouns, many modifies only count nouns, and some/any work with both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Countability patterns differ across languages, so a noun that is noncount in English may be countable in another language.
positions: Cambridge Dictionary: accommodation, advice, furniture, and information are uncountable in English and are not used with a/an or numbers.
Purdue OWL: noncount nouns usually cannot be expressed in a plural form in English.
Cambridge Dictionary: some of these same nouns are countable in other languages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the English pattern and advises checking a learner's dictionary for countability, without presenting other languages' patterns as mistakes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The concrete/abstract labels are a descriptive convention, and some nouns fit both categories.
positions: Wikipedia: concrete nouns name physical entities observable by the senses; abstract nouns name ideas or concepts.
Wikipedia: some nouns, such as art, have both concrete and abstract meanings.
OpenWa Business Grammar: most nouns are things you can see, but nouns can also name ideas such as knowledge or democracy.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents concrete and abstract as useful labels for a real, source-supported distinction and notes that some nouns can shift between the two uses.

sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Provides the capitalization rules for proper nouns (days, months, holidays, names, titles, nationalities, languages, institutions) and a comparison table of common vs proper nouns (museum vs the Art Institute of Chicago). sourceRecords.title: 5.2 Spelling Plural Nouns — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Supports the regular -s rule, -es after s/ch/sh/x/z, the consonant-plus-y to -ies and -f/-fe to -ves patterns, exceptions (roofs, cliffs), and the irregular pairs foot/feet, mouse/mice, person/people. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: 5.3 Apostrophes — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Supports the possessive rules: singular owner adds 's (Adrian's car, the company's profits), plural owner ending in -s adds only the apostrophe (three companies' profits, clients' needs), plural owner not ending in -s adds 's (children's fevers, the people's work), and the warning that apostrophes are rarely used for plurals (Mary's vs Marys vs Marys'). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: 3.1 What Makes a Sentence? — Business Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Supports the subject as the noun or pronoun the sentence is about, the finding-the-subject strategy of removing prepositional phrases, and the object of a preposition as the noun or pronoun that follows the preposition (on the phone; to the office). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Spelling: Plurals — Regular Patterns — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Independent Tier B confirmation that the plural of most nouns is formed by adding s or es and that words ending in -s, -ss, -ch, -sh, or -x take es; also notes the common confusion between plurals and possessives. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Spelling: Plurals — Irregular Patterns — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Independent Tier B confirmation of the consonant-plus-y to -ies and -f/-fe to -ves patterns and of irregular forms learned through exposure, explicitly citing child/children and woman/women as examples. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Parts of Speech — Part 2, Building on Foundations — Language Foundations Handbook
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Defines the subject as the noun or pronoun 'doing' the verb, the object as the word or phrase on the receiving end of the verb, and the object of a preposition as what the preposition references in a prepositional phrase (She returns the book to the library). Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Count and Noncount Nouns: Basic Rules — Purdue OWL
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Supports the count/noncount definitions (count nouns pluralize with -s; noncount nouns usually have no plural: milk, water, air, money, food) and the quantity-word rules: some/any with both, much with noncount only, many with count only. Purdue OWL restricts reproduction; used as reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Nouns: countable and uncountable — English Grammar Today, Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, 2026-08-21). Supports countable nouns as separate countable items with singular/plural forms usable with a/an and numbers, and uncountable nouns as wholes or masses (furniture, water, rice, milk, advice, information, money, work) not used with a/an or numbers and not pluralized; notes that some nouns uncountable in English are countable in other languages. Reference only.
